title: Writing Every Day: You Won't Read it All, Which Is The Point.
subtitle: Relentlessly boring advocacy efforts, explained.
text:
The Frontier Psychiatrists is a daily health-themed newsletter. It’s written by Owen Muir, M.D., and It has a revolutionary agenda: change healthcare, with a focus on problems that are usually considered “mental health problems.” Writing a daily newsletter has been a challenge for me. Today, I’ll write about some of the how and the why.

Subscribe now

Writing an article every day is like a marathon. Marathons are 26-mile foot races to commemorate a particular 26-mile run in ancient Greece, at the end of which the messenger Philippides, in his attempt to thwart a Persian surprise attack on Athens, ran back to deliver crucial news, declaring: "We have won!"), before collapsing and dying.

Endurance sports have risks. Daily writing is no different. Part of my daily writing habit is simple: I wanted to improve. This meant writing more and less time on the under-rewarding topic of “worrying if the writing was good enough.” I have a rule: it has to be good enough. Something goes out every day. Being a perfectionist means less practice, and less practice means my peak is less good than it will be tomorrow.

• I’ve written a lot of pieces you probably haven’t read. People can’t keep up. This is also—buckle up—on purpose. Much of what I write is about systems of care, and I’ve even poked fun at companies by name, which is a great way to have them not like you. “That Owen. Not a Team Player.” A way to mitigate this risk is to write so much that they just don’t read it. With ten articles, reading the one where I roast Private Equity is easy. It gets lost in the inbox with hundreds, and I prefer it this way. I’ve roasted PE more than once, of course.

• I’ve compared PE to the Tin Man in The Wizard of Oz with no heart.

• I’ve had vampires complain about how blood-sucking pales compared to PE acquisitions.

• I’ve had those same vampires parody the term sheets offered by PE.

• I’ve blamed PE for destroying the medical discipline of emergency medicine.

• I’ve made fun of PE for being SO BAD AT BUSINESS that even after rolling up Emergency Medicine, they still went bankrupt.

• I made up my own PE fund that would outperform theirs with some simple math.

Any one of those articles might get me in trouble. But together? Owen continues his quixotic rants about PE…we get it. I want most readers to glaze over. I am sure—because Substack has really good analytics—most readers don't read them all. I also know that some of my readers…do.

It's just a nice tree. © Owen Muir, 2020.

Who reads this newsletter other than you? GREAT question.

I’m an influencer—in that I’m attempting to change decision-making among people who make decisions in health care and how it’s paid for. Many of those individuals read this newsletter. I have just under 3,000 subscribers…but somehow, between 60,000-80,000 reads a month. It’s just under 800,000 reads thus far. Some readers do a deep dive. I often use humor or satire, but some readers take my arguments very seriously.

Share The Frontier Psychiatrists

I’ve written about ERISA compliance quite a bit. I’ll wager most readers roll their eyes— “This is boring!” It is. Boring things also change the world. Very expensive lawsuits with personal liability associated with very wealthy people can motivate a select cohort. My friend Dave Chase has been writing about the coming apocalypse in liability for corporate America for a while:

Jerry Schlichter doesn't mess around. If you listen to interviews with Schlichter, he fights cases to the bitter end even while some of the biggest corporations in history seek to crush him. 2-0 at the Supreme Court with unanimous verdicts speaks for itself.

With over $600 million in settlements that have turned the retirement world upside down, Schlichter is now focusing on #healthcare.

I’m not a lawyer. But I can see the writing on the wall…and write about it.

His is the last list members of the Association of Corporate Counsel want to find themselves on (Schlichter targets -- he's running ads targeting employees of these firms): Anthem, Boston Scientific, Cargill, Caterpillar, CSL Behring, Dollar Tree, Genuine Parts Company, Insperity, Kohl’s, Lockheed Martin, Medical Solutions, MGM Resorts, Nordstrom, Oracle, Performance Food Group, PetSmart, State Farm, Stryker, T-Mobile, Target, Trinity Health, Walgreens.

It is boring, so I don’t write about it every day. You’d never read it if I did. To see change happen, my take is that we need to offer people with a lot of money an option—change how you cover healthcare to include mental health benefits that benefit people with psychiatric illness. Alternatively, you can have class action lawyers and federal regulators dismantle the next decade of your fortune.

It’s very serious. No one would read about that every day. Not enough people anyway. Thus, I write a little something regularly, every day. Some days I write about that. I hope it influences the behavior of people who can make choices that impact all of us to 1. cover their a$$ and 2. champion efforts inside their organizations for a better world.

Thanks for taking a peek behind the curtain!
